claims.text: Within each 4-year period, participants gained an average of 3.35 lb.
Increased daily intake of potato chips is associated with 4-year weight gain.
Increased daily intake of potatoes is associated with 4-year weight gain.
Increased daily intake of sugar-sweetened beverages is associated with 4-year weight gain.
Increased daily intake of unprocessed red meats is associated with 4-year weight gain.
Increased daily intake of processed meats is associated with 4-year weight gain.
Increased daily intake of vegetables is inversely associated with 4-year weight gain.
Increased daily intake of whole grains is inversely associated with 4-year weight gain.
Increased daily intake of fruits is inversely associated with 4-year weight gain.
Increased daily intake of nuts is inversely associated with 4-year weight gain.
Increased daily intake of yogurt is inversely associated with 4-year weight gain.
Increased physical activity is inversely associated with weight gain.
Alcohol consumption is associated with weight gain.
New quitters of smoking experience weight gain.
Sleeping less than 6 hours or more than 8 hours is associated with increased weight gain.
Television watching is associated with weight gain.

evidence.description: Within each 4-year period, participants gained an average of 3.35 lb (5th to 95th percentile, -4.1 to 12.4).
4-year weight change was most strongly associated with the intake of potato chips (1.69 lb per increased daily serving, P<=0.005).
4-year weight change was associated with the intake of potatoes (1.28 lb per increased daily serving, P<=0.005).
4-year weight change was associated with the intake of sugar-sweetened beverages (1.00 lb per increased daily serving, P<=0.005).
4-year weight change was associated with the intake of unprocessed red meats (0.95 lb per increased daily serving, P<=0.005).
4-year weight change was associated with the intake of processed meats (0.93 lb per increased daily serving, P<=0.005).
4-year weight change was inversely associated with the intake of vegetables (-0.22 lb per increased daily serving, P<=0.005).
4-year weight change was inversely associated with the intake of whole grains (-0.37 lb per increased daily serving, P<=0.005).
4-year weight change was inversely associated with the intake of fruits (-0.49 lb per increased daily serving, P<=0.005).
4-year weight change was inversely associated with the intake of nuts (-0.57 lb per increased daily serving, P<=0.005).
4-year weight change was inversely associated with the intake of yogurt (-0.82 lb per increased daily serving, P<=0.005).
Physical activity was independently associated with weight change (-1.76 lb across quintiles, P<0.001).
Alcohol use was independently associated with weight change (0.41 lb per drink per day, P<0.001).
New quitters gained 5.17 lb and former smokers gained 0.14 lb (P<0.001).
More weight gain was observed with <6 or >8 hours of sleep (P<0.001).
Television watching was independently associated with weight change (0.31 lb per hour per day, P<0.001).

methodologies.name: Prospective cohort analysis with pooled inverse-variance-weighted meta-analysis
methodologies.description: Evaluated relationships between changes in lifestyle factors and weight change at 4-year intervals with multivariable adjustments across three prospective cohorts, pooling results via inverse-variance-weighted meta-analysis.
conditions: Participants free of chronic diseases and not obese at baseline
Multivariable adjustments for age, baseline BMI, and lifestyle factors simultaneously
